To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a decrease in recirculation fraction of calcium within myocardial cells, as cardiac temperature increases, underlies an increased oxygen cost of contractility in the canine left and right ventricles.
a temperature-dependent decrease in Ca(2+)-recirculation fraction underlies an increase in O(2) requirement for contractile function of the heart.

the Q(10)s of O(2)-consuming reactions involved in myocardial total Ca2+ handling and in contractility response to it are responsible for the reciprocal Q10 of the recirculation and O(2)-cost of contractility in the canine left heart.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms of myocardial stunning and the role of the recirculation of Ca(2+).
the temperature-dependent changes in the recirculating Ca(2+) pool in the myocardium.
the role of temperature on the energetics of myocardial Ca(2+) homeostasis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a temperature-induced decrease in RF underlies a temperature-dependent increase in O(2) utilization for E(max).
a decrease in RF is a primary mechanism underlying the increase in the O(2) demand of contractility with increasing cardiac temperature.

Q(10), a temperature sensitivity of a physiological process, is the reciprocal of the Q(10), temperature sensitivity of the recirculation of Ca(2+), which in turn is the reciprocal of Q(10) temperature sensitivity of O(2), cost of contractility.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

a decrease in RF of Ca(2+), which would be expected from the temperature-dependent decrease in the rate of Ca(2+)/ATPase of the sarcoplasmic reticulum, underlies the temperature-dependent increase in O(2) demand of contractility in the canine left-ventricle.

temperature changes O(2)-dependent contractile efficiency by changing the balance of ATP-consuming reactions in the myocardial cell, which are involved in Ca( 2+ ) recirculation and contractile response to it.
temperature sensitivity of O(2)-cost of E(max) and RF is reciprocal to each other, which could reflect a reciprocal temperature sensitivity of ATP-consuming reactions for Ca(2+) uptake and release.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the temperature-dependent changes in myocardial energetics and contractility are interrelated.
the temperature sensitivity of the Ca(2+)-handling system in the myocardium is reciprocal to its O(2) efficiency.
the O(2) requirement of the heart is a dynamic parameter that can change in response to a change in the cardiac temperature.
